title: Electrically tunable, two-photon interference from remote silicon-vacancy centers in industrial silicon carbide
authors: Fedor Dzmitryevich Hrunski, Daniel Scheller, Maximilian Hollendonner, Kim Ullerich, Shravan Kumar Parthasarathy, Chiun Fu, Andre Pointner, Wolfgang Knolle, Florian Kaiser, Durga Bhaktavatsala Rao Dasari, Roland Nagy
abstract: Distributed quantum networks rely on spatially separated, independently operated quantum systems as network nodes, whose emitted photons must be interfered with high visibility to establish end-to-end entanglement. Crucially, for network-relevant applications, high visibilities must be achieved over prolonged timescales to reduce overheads for error correction, and to increase network rates. Here, we demonstrate experimentally that silicon vacancy $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ color centers in silicon carbide (SiC) achieve these requirements, notably in a mass-deployable fashion. We integrate $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes, which are controlled via voltage biassing. This way, we demonstrate both, spectral overlapping of 19 randomly selected $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different diodes, as well as spectral narrowing close to the lifetime limit, i.e., typically below 60 MHz. Notably, these performance parameters are long-term stable, e.g., readjusting the p-i-n diode bias is required only every 8.4 hours, which reduces significantly the overall experimental overhead. We then use these assets to demonstrate high-quality two-photon interference between $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers located in two different cryostat setups, which are spatially separated by two meters. Notably, we perform a 26-days long measurement campaign, demonstrating two-photon interference with state-of-the-art raw interference visibilities of 82%, which aligns with the current state-of-the-art. These results establish $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in industry-grade SiC devices as a scalable, spectrally stable building block for distributed quantum networks.
summary: This paper demonstrates the use of electrically tunable silicon vacancy (V_Si) centers in industrial silicon carbide (SiC) as robust quantum nodes. By achieving high-visibility two-photon interference over a 26-day period, the authors establish this platform as a scalable and stable building block for future distributed quantum networks.
main_problem: The core challenge is establishing high-visibility, spectrally stable two-photon interference from spatially separated quantum emitters, which is crucial for building functional distributed quantum networks.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated high-quality two-photon interference with raw visibilities of 82% over a 26-day measurement campaign, using VSi centers embedded in industrially available SiC diodes.
method: The experiment utilized Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry between two remote quantum emitters, combined with active electrical biasing to maintain spectral stability over long periods.
model_or_system: The physical system is the silicon vacancy (V_Si) color center embedded in industrial-grade 4H silicon carbide (SiC) p-i-n diodes. These centers act as solid-state quantum nodes whose emission can be tuned and stabilized electrically.
key_observables: Two-photon interference visibility (82%), spectral linewidths (below 60 MHz), and long-term stability (bias readjustment every 8.4 hours).
important_parameters: Two-meter spatial separation, 26-day measurement duration, and the linear tuning coefficient of the A2 transition frequency with voltage bias.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the cross-correlation data using established quantum interference formulas, and the stability is demonstrated through long-term electrical control of the emitter frequency.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the VSi center's optical contrast, the p-i-n diode structure, PLE spectra showing linewidths, and the experimental setup for the two-photon interference measurement across separated cryostats.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing the VSi centers' tunability and spectral narrowing in SiC diodes, to demonstrating single-photon purity, and finally to performing and analyzing the two-photon interference measurement over an extended, stable period.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly scalable, solid-state platform for quantum networking, directly addressing the engineering hurdles (stability, integration) that limit the deployment of quantum repeaters.
